records.question: Japan: if a bank or payment system fails, who takes the loss, in what order?
records.answer: On the Japan money map (as of September 15, 2026), a failure moves through 5 separate steps: what sets it off (Ordinary liquidity stress, Operational outage, Systemic failure classification); the private first response (Commercial banks, Japan Securities Clearing Corporation, Zengin System and More Time, FMI default waterfalls); the Bank of Japan's liquidity step (BOJ Policy Board, BOJ current-account balances, BOJ-NET Funds Transfer System, BOJ Article 33 lending, BOJ Article 37 outage lending, BOJ Article 38 special support), which lends against collateral and does not cover a final loss; resolution (Cabinet and Prime Minister, Financial Services Agency, Deposit Insurance Corporation of Japan, TLAC and creditor loss, Deposit protection and transfer); and where the loss finally lands (Fraud compensation and restitution, JPYSC trust stablecoin, Possible retail CBDC, Industry contributions, Conditional fiscal subsidy or guarantee). Public money is a last, conditional step that needs legal and budget approval.

records.question: Where do Korea's won stablecoin and Han River project stand?
records.answer: The won stablecoin still has no law: the Korea country file says that as of October 3, 2026 South Korea had no enacted general public-won stablecoin regime, and that a future won stablecoin's issuer, reserves and redemption rules were unresolved. In the world money record, the Digital Asset Basic Act was introduced June 10, 2025, stalled December 30, 2025 over who may issue the token, the government proposed its own bill April 8, 2026, and on May 12, 2026 it was left off the National Policy Committee's last agenda before recess. The Bank of Korea paused Phase 2 of Project Han River (Hangang), its wholesale CBDC and tokenized-deposit trial with the banks, on June 26, 2025, and relaunched it March 18, 2026 with nine banks, retooled around tokenizing government disbursements; on July 1, 2026 the Bank floated growing it into foreign-bond investment infrastructure; and on July 15, 2026 its Phase II designation was expanded, with Kyongnam and iM Bank newly designated. The country file treats Hangang tokens as commercial-bank deposit claims in a controlled pilot; no public-won issuer or production wholesale CBDC was established.

records.question: Which payment rails are being rebuilt around Swift, or alongside it?
records.answer: The world record holds 35 dated payment-plumbing moves in 10 regions, January 6, 2025 to July 7, 2026: China's CIPS signing foreign banks, BRICS Pay targeted for a pilot, Africa's PAPSS, Indonesia's QRIS reaching Japan, Korea and China, Project Nexus, and the ECB's Pontes and Appia links. Swift's own shared ledger has four readings: announced September 29, 2025; 'controlled initial use preparing' on the Japan map (September 15, 2026); 'MVP ready; pilots pending', grade M4, on the UK map (September 14, 2026); and, newest, 17 listed banks and 6 bank-published pilot transactions (October 19, 2026).

records.question: UK: which documents legally control a stablecoin, digital gilt or tokenised fund, and which are still missing?
records.answer: Of 26 documents that control UK stablecoins, the digital gilt (DIGIT), tokenised funds and settlement (UK map, as of September 14, 2026), 10 are in force or final, 3 are drafts or open, and 13 are required but not published, not located or not yet inspected — among them the HSBC Gate 2 finality self-attestation, the DIGIT platform-provider appointment, the HSBC–LSEG bilateral DSD memorandum.

records.question: Who can make law for each part of the UK and its territories?
records.answer: The UK Parliament can make law for the whole UK ('Parliamentary sovereignty within the UK constitutional order'). It has handed law-making for devolved matters to three legislatures: the Scottish Parliament (Scotland Act 1998 as amended), Senedd Cymru (Government of Wales Act 2006 as amended) and the Northern Ireland Assembly (Northern Ireland Act 1998 and Agreement settlement). England has no legislature of its own on the map: it is 'predominantly governed through UK institutions, local government and devolved local arrangements'. The 3 Crown Dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man) and 14 British Overseas Territories are not part of the UK. The Crown Dependencies are self-governing under island constitutional law (Jersey answers to its States Assembly, the Isle of Man to Tynwald), linked through the Crown, with the Privy Council handling 'Royal Assent and specified Crown functions'. Each Overseas Territory runs under its own constitution or Orders within the UK constitutional framework, with a Governor or Commissioner; the map does not name each territory's legislature.

records.question: UK: how far has each on-ledger money, gilt or settlement project got?
records.answer: Of 15 UK on-ledger money, gilt and settlement projects on the UK map (as of September 14, 2026), the furthest along is the Tokenised authorised-fund register at M7 (authoritative-record integration); 1 at M5 (limited production); 10 at M4 (authorised or production-bound); 2 at M1 (technical prototype or design work); 1 at M0 (concept or policy intention). The least advanced: HSBC–LSEG DSD link, Digital pound design phase, Bank of England Synchronisation Lab. No project has reached M8 or above (liquidity integration, proven failure and exit, normal infrastructure).

records.question: Who runs the City of London and UK public money?
records.answer: HM Treasury runs UK public money: it administers the UK Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund and the Debt Management Account and owns the Exchange Equalisation Account, the Bank of England and The Royal Mint; the Bank of England (whose capital is held for Treasury, with statutory independence) operates RTGS / CHAPS and acts as Treasury's agent for the Exchange Equalisation Account. Parliament legislates for 'tax, Supply and financial-services law', and the National Audit Office serves it. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each keep their own consolidated fund, answerable to their legislature. The City of London is run by the City of London Corporation, through the Court of Common Council and the Court of Aldermen; it keeps the City Fund, the City's Estate and the City Bridge Foundation separate, and it 'does not set UK tax, regulate UK finance or constitute a state within a state.' It is a different body from the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London. 'The City' as a financial market is not a legal person: the FCA and the PRA regulate the firms in it.

records.question: How does a UN decision get made, paid for and carried out, and who controls each step?
records.answer: A General Assembly decision passes through 13 steps, each with its own controller: Member States authorize; a state, organ or the Secretary-General asks for an agenda item; the General Committee filters it; a Main Committee takes the work; sponsors and co-facilitators write the text; the Assembly adopts it (two thirds for budget and other important questions, a simple majority otherwise); then the Fifth Committee and ACABQ decide the money, the Secretary-General carries it out, and auditors and Member States review it. Adoption is not funding, and funding is not delivery.
